stem: In economics, the 'environment' refers to:
options: the total planetary inheritance (all the surroundings) — including all the biotic and abiotic elements (land, water, air, living things) that support life
solution: In economics (and environmental studies), the 'environment' refers to the total planetary inheritance and the totality of all the resources and surroundings — it includes all the biotic elements (living things — plants, animals, micro-organisms) and abiotic elements (non-living things — land, water, air, sunlight, minerals) that surround and support life. So the environment is the whole set of natural surroundings and resources within which humans and other living things exist and on which they depend. Understanding this broad meaning of the environment is a prelims point. In economics, the environment is the total planetary inheritance — all the biotic and abiotic elements (land, water, air, living things) that support life.

stem: The environment performs several vital functions for us, including supplying resources, assimilating (absorbing) waste, sustaining life, and:
solution: The environment performs several vital functions: (1) it supplies resources — both renewable resources (like forests, water, which can be replenished) and non-renewable resources (like minerals, fossil fuels, which get exhausted); (2) it assimilates (absorbs and breaks down) waste — acting as a sink for the waste and pollution generated by human activity; (3) it sustains life — by providing the essentials for life (like the genetic and biodiversity resources, clean air, water, and the conditions for life — the sun, the ozone layer, etc.); and (4) it provides aesthetic and other services — like natural beauty, scenery, recreation, and enjoyment (and cultural/spiritual value). These functions show how essential the environment is to human life and the economy. Understanding the functions of the environment is a prelims point. The environment supplies resources, assimilates waste, sustains life, and provides aesthetic and other services.

stem: The environment is able to perform its functions (like providing resources and absorbing waste) without harm only so long as the demands on it are within its __________ (its capacity to supply and absorb).
solution: The environment is able to perform its functions (supplying resources, absorbing waste, sustaining life) without being harmed or degraded only so long as the demands placed on it stay within its 'carrying capacity' — that is, the maximum load (of resource extraction and waste) that the environment can bear/sustain without being damaged. As long as we do not take resources faster than they can be regenerated, and do not generate waste faster than the environment can absorb it (i.e., we stay within the carrying capacity), the environment stays healthy. But when the demands exceed the carrying capacity — as has happened with the rising population and consumption — the environment gets degraded (resources are depleted, and waste/pollution accumulates), leading to an 'environmental crisis'. Understanding the carrying capacity is a key prelims point. The environment can perform its functions without harm only so long as the demands on it stay within its carrying capacity.

stem: An environmental crisis (like pollution and resource depletion) arises when the demands on the environment __________ its carrying capacity.
solution: An environmental crisis arises when the demands placed on the environment exceed (become more than) its carrying capacity — that is, when we extract resources faster than they can be regenerated, and generate waste/pollution faster than the environment can absorb and neutralise it. When this happens (as with the huge rise in population, consumption, and industrial activity), the environment can no longer cope: resources get depleted/exhausted, and pollution and waste accumulate — degrading the air, water, land, and ecosystems. This over-exploitation of the environment (beyond its carrying capacity) is the root of the present-day environmental crisis (pollution, resource depletion, global warming, loss of biodiversity, etc.). Understanding that the crisis arises when demands exceed carrying capacity is a key prelims point. An environmental crisis arises when the demands on the environment exceed its carrying capacity.

stem: Resources that CAN be replenished/renewed by natural processes (if used wisely) — like forests, water, and fisheries — are called:
solution: Renewable resources are those natural resources that can be replenished, renewed, or regenerated by natural processes within a reasonable time (if they are used wisely and not over-exploited) — such as forests (trees regrow), water (renewed by the water cycle), fisheries (fish reproduce), soil, and solar/wind energy. As long as such resources are used at a rate within their regeneration capacity, they can last indefinitely. (However, if they are over-exploited — used faster than they can regenerate — even renewable resources can be depleted or destroyed.) This contrasts with non-renewable resources (like minerals and fossil fuels), which get exhausted. Understanding renewable resources is a prelims point. Renewable resources (like forests, water, fisheries) can be replenished/renewed by natural processes, if used wisely.

stem: Resources that get EXHAUSTED with use and cannot be replenished (or take millions of years to form) — like coal, petroleum, and minerals — are called:
solution: Non-renewable resources are those natural resources that get exhausted/used up with use and cannot be replenished within a human time-scale (they either do not regenerate at all, or take millions of years to form) — such as the fossil fuels (coal, petroleum/oil, natural gas) and the mineral ores (iron, copper, etc.). Once these are used up, they are gone (for practical purposes). Because they are finite and exhaustible, non-renewable resources must be used carefully and conserved, and alternatives (like renewable energy) developed — otherwise they will run out. This contrasts with renewable resources (like forests, water), which can regenerate. Understanding non-renewable resources is a prelims point. Non-renewable resources (like coal, petroleum, and minerals) get exhausted with use and cannot be replenished (or take millions of years to form).

stem: The addition of harmful substances (contaminants) to the air, water, or land, making it dirty/unfit, is called:
solution: Pollution is the addition/introduction of harmful or unwanted substances (contaminants/pollutants) — such as smoke, chemicals, sewage, industrial waste, plastics, and noise — into the environment (the air, water, or land), making it dirty, contaminated, and unfit or harmful (for living things and human use). The main types include air pollution, water pollution, land/soil pollution, and noise pollution. Pollution is one of the major forms of environmental degradation, harming health, ecosystems, and the quality of life, and it results largely from human activities (industry, vehicles, waste). Understanding pollution (contamination of the environment) is a prelims point. Pollution is the addition of harmful substances to the air, water, or land, making it dirty/unfit.

stem: Sustainable development is defined as development that meets the needs of the present generation without compromising the ability of __________ to meet their own needs.
solution: Sustainable development is famously defined (by the Brundtland Commission's report 'Our Common Future') as 'development that meets the needs of the present generation without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.' The key idea is that development (economic growth and the improvement of living standards) should be pursued in a way that does not deplete the resources or degrade the environment to the point where future generations are left worse off — i.e., we should use resources and the environment wisely and sustainably, so that they remain available for our children and grandchildren too. So sustainable development balances the needs of the present with the interests of the future (and with environmental protection). Understanding the definition of sustainable development is a key prelims point. Sustainable development meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.

stem: Sustainable development requires balancing economic development with __________.
solution: Sustainable development requires balancing economic development (growth, raising incomes and living standards) with environmental protection (conserving natural resources and protecting the environment) — and also with social equity (fairness, so that development benefits all, including the poor and future generations). It recognises that economic development and the environment are not opposed but interdependent: development that destroys the environment is not sustainable (it undermines its own future basis), and protecting the environment while ignoring the needs of the poor is also not workable. So sustainable development seeks a balance — pursuing development in an environmentally sound and socially fair way, so that it can be continued into the future. Understanding this balancing of development and environment (and equity) is a key prelims point. Sustainable development requires balancing economic development with environmental protection (and social equity).

stem: The 'Green Revolution', while boosting food production, harmed the environment by causing:
options: the overuse of chemical fertilisers and pesticides (degrading the soil and polluting water) and the over-extraction of groundwater
solution: The Green Revolution, while greatly boosting India's food-grain production (and achieving food self-sufficiency), harmed the environment in several ways: the heavy overuse of chemical fertilisers and pesticides degraded the soil (reducing its natural fertility, and leaving chemical residues) and polluted the water (fertiliser and pesticide runoff contaminating rivers, ponds, and groundwater); and the water-intensive HYV crops led to the over-extraction/depletion of groundwater (falling water tables) in the Green Revolution regions. It also contributed to the loss of biodiversity (as diverse traditional crops were replaced by a few HYV crops). So the Green Revolution is an example of how a development achievement had serious environmental costs — highlighting the need for sustainable agriculture. Understanding the environmental harm of the Green Revolution is a prelims point. The Green Revolution harmed the environment through the overuse of chemical fertilisers/pesticides (degrading soil and polluting water) and the over-extraction of groundwater.

stem: The depletion of India's __________ (falling water tables) due to over-extraction (for irrigation, etc.) is a serious environmental problem.
solution: The depletion of groundwater (the falling of water tables — the underground water level dropping lower and lower) due to the over-extraction of groundwater (pumping out more than is naturally recharged), especially for irrigation (and also for drinking and industry), is a serious environmental problem in India. In many regions (especially the intensively-farmed Green Revolution areas), so much groundwater has been drawn out that the water tables have fallen drastically, wells have dried up, and water has become scarce (and sometimes contaminated). This over-exploitation of the finite groundwater is unsustainable and threatens future water security. Measures like rainwater harvesting and efficient water use are needed to address it. Understanding groundwater depletion as an environmental problem is a prelims-relevant point. The depletion of groundwater (falling water tables) due to over-extraction is a serious environmental problem in India.

stem: India faces the problem of land degradation, including __________, in which fertile land is turned into desert due to overuse, drought, and deforestation.
solution: India faces serious problems of land degradation — the decline in the quality and productivity of the land — one form of which is desertification: the process by which fertile/productive land is degraded and turned into desert (barren land), due to a combination of factors such as the overuse of the land (over-cultivation and overgrazing), prolonged drought, deforestation, and poor land and water management (which strip the vegetation and erode/degrade the soil). Land degradation and desertification reduce the land available for agriculture, threaten food security and livelihoods, and worsen poverty — making them a major environmental and developmental concern (addressed by soil and water conservation, afforestation, and better land use). Understanding desertification (as land degradation) is a prelims-relevant point. Desertification is the turning of fertile land into desert due to overuse, drought, and deforestation — a form of land degradation in India.

stem: The rise in the Earth's temperature due to the increase of greenhouse gases (a major global environmental problem) is called:
solution: Global warming (and the wider phenomenon of climate change) is the rise in the average temperature of the Earth's atmosphere and oceans, caused by the increase in the concentration of greenhouse gases (like carbon dioxide and methane) in the atmosphere due to human activities (burning fossil fuels, deforestation, industry). It is one of the most serious global environmental problems, with consequences such as the melting of glaciers and ice caps, rising sea levels, more extreme and unpredictable weather (droughts, floods, storms, heat waves), and harm to agriculture, ecosystems, and human life. Global warming is a central concern of sustainable development (requiring the reduction of greenhouse-gas emissions). Understanding global warming as a major environmental problem is a prelims point. Global warming (climate change) is the rise in the Earth's temperature due to increasing greenhouse gases — a major global environmental problem.

stem: The thinning of the ozone layer (which protects us from harmful UV rays), caused by chemicals like CFCs, is called ozone:
solution: Ozone depletion is the thinning/reduction of the ozone layer in the stratosphere — the layer that shields the Earth from most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation. It is caused chiefly by human-made chemicals, especially the chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs, used in refrigerators, air-conditioners, and aerosols) and related substances, which destroy ozone molecules. Ozone depletion (including the 'ozone hole' over Antarctica) is a serious global environmental problem, because a thinner ozone layer lets more harmful UV radiation reach the surface, causing skin cancer, cataracts, harm to the immune system, and damage to plants, crops, and marine life. (It is being addressed by the Montreal Protocol, which phases out CFCs.) Understanding ozone depletion as an environmental problem is a prelims point. Ozone depletion is the thinning of the ozone layer (which shields us from UV rays), caused by chemicals like CFCs.

stem: Some strategies for sustainable development include using non-conventional (renewable) energy sources, such as:
options: solar, wind, and hydro (and bio-gas) energy
solution: A key strategy for sustainable development is the use of non-conventional (renewable, clean) sources of energy — instead of, or in addition to, the polluting and exhaustible fossil fuels (coal, oil, gas). These renewable energy sources include: solar energy (from the sun); wind energy (from wind, using windmills/turbines); hydro (hydroelectric) energy (from flowing water); and bio-gas (from organic/animal waste, e.g., gobar gas plants in villages) — as well as tidal and geothermal energy. These sources are renewable (inexhaustible) and clean (much less polluting), so shifting to them helps conserve the finite fossil fuels and reduce pollution and global warming — supporting sustainable development. Understanding the use of renewable energy as a sustainability strategy is a prelims point. Sustainable development strategies include using non-conventional (renewable) energy like solar, wind, hydro, and bio-gas.

stem: The strategy of 'Reduce, Reuse, Recycle' (the 3 Rs) helps sustainable development by:
options: minimising waste and the use of resources (using less, using things again, and recovering materials)
solution: The strategy of the '3 Rs' — Reduce, Reuse, Recycle — helps sustainable development by minimising waste and the wasteful use of resources: Reduce means using fewer resources and generating less waste in the first place (consuming less, avoiding wasteful use); Reuse means using things again (rather than throwing them away after one use); and Recycle means recovering and reprocessing the materials from used/waste products to make new products (instead of using fresh raw materials). Together, the 3 Rs conserve natural resources, reduce pollution and the mountains of waste, and lessen the burden on the environment — helping to make development more sustainable. Understanding the 3 Rs (Reduce, Reuse, Recycle) is a prelims-relevant point. The 3 Rs (Reduce, Reuse, Recycle) support sustainable development by minimising waste and the use of resources.

stem: The use of bio-gas plants (producing gas from cow-dung and other organic waste) in rural areas is an example of a __________ strategy for development.
solution: The use of bio-gas plants — which produce bio-gas (a clean-burning fuel, mainly methane) from cow-dung and other organic/animal waste (through the action of bacteria) — in rural areas is an example of a sustainable development strategy. It is sustainable because: it provides clean energy (for cooking and lighting) from a renewable resource (organic waste, which is continuously produced), reducing the need for firewood (saving forests) and fossil fuels, and reducing pollution and smoke (better for health and the environment); and the leftover slurry can be used as good organic manure (fertiliser). So bio-gas plants make productive, clean use of a renewable waste resource, benefiting both the people and the environment — an example of sustainable development. Understanding bio-gas as a sustainable strategy is a prelims-relevant point. Bio-gas plants (making clean gas from cow-dung/organic waste) in rural areas are an example of a sustainable development strategy.

stem: A traditional Indian system of water conservation (harvesting and storing rainwater for use), which supports sustainable water management, is:
solution: Rainwater harvesting — the collecting and storing of rainwater (in tanks, ponds, reservoirs, or by letting it soak into the ground to recharge groundwater), for later use — is a traditional and effective method of water conservation that supports sustainable water management. By capturing the rain (which would otherwise run off and be lost) and storing it (or recharging the groundwater with it), rainwater harvesting provides water for use in dry periods, reduces the over-extraction and depletion of groundwater, and helps cope with water scarcity — all in a sustainable way. India has many traditional rainwater-harvesting systems, and it is being revived and promoted as a key water-conservation strategy. Understanding rainwater harvesting (as a sustainable water strategy) is a prelims-relevant point. Rainwater harvesting (collecting and storing rainwater) is a traditional method of water conservation supporting sustainable water management.

stem: Sustainable development is important because the current path of development (with over-exploitation of resources and pollution) is:
options: unsustainable — it degrades the environment and depletes resources, threatening the well-being of future generations (and even the present)
solution: Sustainable development is important because the current/conventional path of development — with its over-exploitation of natural resources (depleting forests, water, minerals, and fossil fuels) and its heavy pollution and environmental degradation — is unsustainable: it is degrading and destroying the very environmental basis on which development and life depend, and depleting the resources, so that if it continues, it will leave a degraded, resource-poor, and dangerous world for future generations (and it is already harming the present, through pollution, climate change, water scarcity, etc.). In other words, this path cannot be sustained/continued into the future without disaster. So there is an urgent need to switch to a sustainable path — one that meets present needs while protecting the environment and resources for the future. Understanding why sustainable development is needed (the current path is unsustainable) is a key prelims point. Sustainable development is important because the current path (over-exploiting resources and polluting) is unsustainable, threatening future (and present) well-being.

stem: Assertion (A): Economic development and environmental protection must go together (sustainable development). Reason (R): Development that destroys the environment ultimately undermines its own resource base and harms the well-being of present and future generations. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that economic development and environmental protection must go together — this is the essence of sustainable development. And the reason is (R) that development which destroys/degrades the environment ultimately undermines its own resource base (development depends on natural resources — land, water, forests, minerals, a stable climate — so destroying these destroys the basis for future development) and harms the well-being of both present and future generations (through pollution, resource scarcity, climate change, disasters, and ill-health). So, because environmental destruction is self-defeating and harmful, development cannot be pursued at the cost of the environment — the two must go together — R correctly explains A. Understanding why development and environmental protection must go together is a key prelims point. Development and environmental protection must go together because development that destroys the environment undermines its own resource base and harms present and future generations.

stem: The famous definition of sustainable development comes from the report 'Our Common Future' (1987), produced by the __________ Commission.
options: Brundtland (World Commission on Environment and Development)
solution: The famous definition of sustainable development — 'development that meets the needs of the present generation without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs' — comes from the report 'Our Common Future' (1987), produced by the World Commission on Environment and Development, popularly known as the Brundtland Commission (after its chairperson, Gro Harlem Brundtland, then the Prime Minister of Norway). This report brought the concept of sustainable development to worldwide prominence. Understanding that the Brundtland Commission ('Our Common Future', 1987) gave the definition of sustainable development is a prelims-relevant point. The definition of sustainable development comes from the Brundtland Commission's report 'Our Common Future' (1987).

stem: The Earth Summit (United Nations Conference on Environment and Development) that gave a major boost to sustainable development was held in 1992 in:
solution: The Earth Summit — the United Nations Conference on Environment and Development (UNCED) — that gave a major boost to the idea of sustainable development was held in 1992 in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. This landmark global conference brought together leaders from around the world to address environment and development issues together, and it produced important outcomes — such as Agenda 21 (a global action plan for sustainable development), and the frameworks that led to conventions on climate change (UNFCCC) and biodiversity. The Rio Earth Summit (1992) was a milestone in global environmental cooperation and the promotion of sustainable development. Understanding the 1992 Rio Earth Summit is a prelims-relevant point. The Earth Summit that boosted sustainable development was held in 1992 in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil.

stem: The principle that those who cause pollution should bear the cost of cleaning it up / the damage it causes is called the __________ principle.
solution: The 'Polluter Pays' principle is the environmental principle that those who cause/produce the pollution should bear the cost (be made to pay for) cleaning it up and/or for the damage/harm it causes to the environment and to others. The idea is to make the polluters responsible and accountable for their pollution (rather than letting them dump the costs onto society or the environment for free) — which also gives them an incentive to reduce their pollution. This principle is widely used in environmental policy and law (e.g., through pollution taxes, fines, and clean-up liabilities). Understanding the 'polluter pays' principle is a prelims-relevant point. The 'polluter pays' principle holds that those who cause pollution should bear the cost of cleaning it up or the damage it causes.

stem: Pollution can be seen as a 'negative externality' — a harmful cost imposed on __________ by the polluter (who does not bear the full cost).
solution: Pollution is an example of a 'negative externality' — a harmful cost/effect that an economic activity (like a factory's production) imposes on others (third parties)/society at large, who are not part of the transaction, and for which the polluter does not pay (does not bear the full cost). For example, a factory that pollutes a river harms the people downstream (their health, water, fishing) — but if the factory is not made to pay for this harm, it 'externalises' this cost onto society, while enjoying the profits itself. Because the polluter does not bear these external costs, the market over-produces pollution (there is 'market failure'). This is why the government must intervene (e.g., through regulation, taxes, or the 'polluter pays' principle) to make polluters account for these external costs. Understanding pollution as a negative externality is a prelims-relevant point. Pollution is a 'negative externality' — a harmful cost imposed on others/society by the polluter, who does not bear the full cost.

stem: The idea that sustainable development requires fairness BETWEEN generations (not using up resources so as to leave future generations worse off) is called __________ equity.
solution: Inter-generational equity is the idea/principle that sustainable development requires fairness between different generations — that the present generation should not use up the resources or degrade the environment in a way that leaves the future generations worse off (deprived of the resources and the healthy environment they need to meet their own needs). In other words, we hold the Earth in trust for our descendants, and we must pass it on to them in a fit condition. This concern for the future generations (inter-generational equity) is at the heart of the definition of sustainable development. (There is also 'intra-generational equity' — fairness among people within the present generation, e.g., between the rich and the poor.) Understanding inter-generational equity is a prelims-relevant point. Inter-generational equity is fairness between generations — not using up resources so as to leave future generations worse off.

stem: The problem in which a resource that is open to all (a 'commons', like a common grazing land or a fishery) tends to be over-used and degraded because no one owns or protects it, is called:
solution: The 'tragedy of the commons' is the problem in which a common-property resource — a resource that is open to everyone and owned by no one in particular (like a common grazing land, a public forest, a fishery, or the air/water) — tends to be over-used, exploited, and degraded/destroyed. This happens because each individual user, acting in their own self-interest, tries to take as much as they can (since if they don't, someone else will), and no one has the responsibility or incentive to protect and conserve the resource for the future — so the collective result is over-exploitation and ruin of the shared resource. This is a key reason why open-access environmental resources get degraded, and why some form of regulation, community management, or collective action is needed to protect them. Understanding the 'tragedy of the commons' is a prelims-relevant point. The 'tragedy of the commons' is the over-use and degradation of a shared, open-access resource because no one owns or protects it.

stem: The largest source of solar energy promotion, an alliance co-founded by India to promote solar power globally, is the:
solution: The International Solar Alliance (ISA) is a global alliance/coalition, co-founded by India (along with France), to promote the use of solar energy worldwide — especially among the sun-rich countries (those between the tropics). Its aim is to mobilise investment, technology, and cooperation to expand solar power, reduce dependence on fossil fuels, and combat climate change. India's leadership of the ISA reflects its push toward renewable (solar) energy as part of sustainable development and its response to climate change. (India has ambitious solar-energy targets.) Understanding the International Solar Alliance (India-led, for solar energy) is a prelims-relevant point. The International Solar Alliance (ISA), co-founded by India, promotes solar power globally.

stem: The requirement that large development projects (like dams, mines, factories) must be assessed in advance for their likely effects on the environment is called an:
solution: An Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) is the process/requirement by which the likely environmental effects (impacts) of a proposed large development project — such as a dam, mine, factory, highway, or power plant — are studied and assessed in advance (before the project is approved and built). The aim is to identify and evaluate the possible harmful effects on the environment (on air, water, land, forests, wildlife, and people), and to ensure that these are taken into account in deciding whether and how to go ahead with the project, and to plan measures to prevent or reduce the harm. EIA is thus a key tool for integrating environmental concerns into development decisions (for sustainable development). Understanding EIA (assessing projects' environmental effects in advance) is a prelims-relevant point. An Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) assesses in advance the likely environmental effects of a large development project.

stem: The over-cutting of forests (deforestation) is an environmental problem because forests __________.
options: provide many benefits (oxygen, absorbing CO2, wildlife habitat, soil and water conservation, biodiversity), so losing them harms the environment
solution: The over-cutting of forests (deforestation) is a serious environmental problem because forests provide many vital benefits and functions, so their loss harms the environment in many ways. Forests: release oxygen and absorb carbon dioxide (so their loss worsens global warming and air quality); are the habitat of wildlife and the store of biodiversity (so deforestation causes the loss of species/biodiversity); conserve the soil (their roots prevent erosion) and water (they help rainwater soak in, recharge groundwater, and regulate rivers) — so their loss leads to soil erosion, floods, and water problems; and influence the climate and rainfall. So cutting down forests damages the whole web of environmental benefits they provide — which is why deforestation is a major environmental concern, and afforestation and forest conservation are important. Understanding why deforestation harms the environment is a prelims point. Deforestation harms the environment because forests provide oxygen, absorb CO2, shelter wildlife, and conserve soil and water — benefits lost when they are cut.

stem: The loss of the variety of plant and animal species (due to habitat destruction, pollution, etc.) is called the loss of:
solution: The loss of biodiversity is the reduction/loss of the variety of living things — the different species of plants, animals, and micro-organisms (and the variety of genes and ecosystems) — on the Earth. It is caused by human activities such as the destruction of habitats (deforestation, draining wetlands, etc.), pollution, over-exploitation (over-hunting, over-fishing), the introduction of invasive species, and climate change. Biodiversity loss is a serious environmental problem, because biodiversity is valuable (for ecological balance, food, medicines, and the stability and functioning of ecosystems), and the extinction of species is irreversible. Conserving biodiversity (through protected areas, etc.) is an important part of environmental protection and sustainable development. Understanding biodiversity loss as an environmental problem is a prelims point. The loss of biodiversity is the loss of the variety of plant and animal species, due to habitat destruction, pollution, etc.

stem: Air pollution in Indian cities (a serious problem, e.g., in Delhi) is caused largely by:
options: vehicle exhaust, industrial emissions, burning of fuels/crop residue, and dust
solution: Air pollution in Indian cities (a very serious problem, notoriously in Delhi and other big cities) is caused largely by human activities that release pollutants into the air, such as: the exhaust from the growing number of vehicles (cars, trucks, buses); the emissions from industries and factories; the burning of fossil fuels (coal, etc.) for power and other uses; the burning of crop residue (stubble) in nearby farms (a major seasonal cause in north India); the burning of waste; and construction and road dust. This pollution creates smog and high levels of harmful particles and gases in the air, causing serious health problems (especially respiratory diseases). Controlling these sources (cleaner vehicles and fuels, controlling industrial emissions and crop-burning, etc.) is needed to reduce air pollution. Understanding the causes of urban air pollution is a prelims-relevant point. Urban air pollution in India is caused largely by vehicle exhaust, industrial emissions, the burning of fuels/crop residue, and dust.

stem: The mission launched by the government to clean and rejuvenate the river Ganga is:
solution: 'Namami Gange' (the National Mission for Clean Ganga) is the flagship programme/mission launched by the government to clean, protect, and rejuvenate the river Ganga — which had become heavily polluted (from sewage, industrial waste, and other sources). The mission involves measures such as building sewage-treatment plants (to stop untreated sewage from entering the river), controlling industrial pollution, cleaning the river surface and ghats, afforestation along the banks, and promoting public awareness. It reflects the effort to tackle the serious water pollution of India's rivers (an important environmental problem). Understanding the Namami Gange mission (cleaning the Ganga) is a prelims-relevant point. 'Namami Gange' is the government mission to clean and rejuvenate the polluted river Ganga.

stem: The government's nationwide campaign for cleanliness and sanitation (building toilets, ending open defecation, managing waste) is the __________ Mission.
solution: The Swachh Bharat Mission (Clean India Mission) is the government's nationwide campaign for cleanliness and sanitation — aimed at making India clean by building toilets (to end open defecation, which was a major public-health and environmental problem), improving the management of solid and liquid waste, and promoting hygiene and cleanliness in both rural and urban areas. Better sanitation and waste management improve public health, protect water sources from contamination, and improve the environment — supporting both human well-being and sustainable development. Understanding the Swachh Bharat Mission (cleanliness/sanitation) is a prelims-relevant point. The Swachh Bharat Mission is the government's campaign for cleanliness and sanitation (toilets, ending open defecation, waste management).

stem: India's plan to address climate change through eight national missions (including on solar energy, energy efficiency, water, etc.) is the National Action Plan on __________.
solution: The National Action Plan on Climate Change (NAPCC) is India's comprehensive plan/strategy to address climate change, launched in 2008. It works through eight national 'missions' focused on key areas — such as the National Solar Mission (promoting solar energy), the National Mission for Enhanced Energy Efficiency, the National Water Mission (water conservation), the National Mission for a Green India (afforestation), the National Mission for Sustainable Agriculture, the National Mission for Sustaining the Himalayan Ecosystem, the National Mission on Sustainable Habitat, and the Mission on Strategic Knowledge for Climate Change. Through these missions, the NAPCC aims to promote sustainable development while addressing climate change (both adapting to it and reducing emissions). Understanding the NAPCC (India's climate-change action plan) is a prelims-relevant point. The National Action Plan on Climate Change (NAPCC) addresses climate change through eight national missions (on solar, energy efficiency, water, etc.).

stem: Efficient methods of irrigation that save water (using much less than flooding the fields) include drip irrigation and __________ irrigation.
solution: Efficient (water-saving) methods of irrigation — which deliver water to crops using much less water than the traditional method of flooding the fields — include: drip irrigation (water is delivered drop by drop, slowly, directly to the roots of the plants, through a network of pipes/tubes, minimising waste) and sprinkler irrigation (water is sprayed over the crops like rain, through sprinklers, covering the field more evenly and using less water than flooding). These methods conserve water (very important given India's water scarcity and groundwater depletion), and they also reduce problems like waterlogging and salinity. Promoting such efficient irrigation is an important sustainable-development strategy for water. Understanding drip and sprinkler irrigation (water-saving methods) is a prelims-relevant point. Efficient water-saving irrigation methods include drip irrigation and sprinkler irrigation.

stem: The environmental problem in which rain becomes acidic (due to pollutant gases like sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides), harming plants, water bodies, and buildings, is called:
solution: Acid rain is the environmental problem in which rain (and other precipitation) becomes acidic — that is, the rainwater has a higher-than-normal acidity. It is caused by air pollution: the emission of gases like sulphur dioxide (SO2) and nitrogen oxides (NOx) — mainly from the burning of fossil fuels (in power plants, industries, and vehicles) — which react with water vapour in the atmosphere to form acids (sulphuric and nitric acids), which then fall with the rain. Acid rain harms the environment: it damages plants and forests, acidifies lakes and rivers (killing fish and aquatic life), degrades the soil, and corrodes buildings, monuments, and structures (e.g., harming the Taj Mahal). It is another consequence of air pollution. Understanding acid rain is a prelims-relevant point. Acid rain is rain made acidic by pollutant gases (SO2, NOx), which harms plants, water bodies, and buildings.

stem: The concept of environmental accounting / 'green GDP' tries to measure economic growth after taking into account:
options: the depletion of natural resources and the cost of environmental damage (so that growth that harms the environment is not counted as pure gain)
solution: The concept of environmental accounting / 'green GDP' tries to measure a country's economic growth/output after taking into account (deducting/adjusting for) the depletion of natural resources and the cost of environmental damage (degradation and pollution) caused by economic activity. The idea is that the conventional GDP measure counts all production as 'gain', ignoring the fact that some of that production degrades the environment and uses up natural resources (which is a real cost/loss). 'Green GDP' or environmental accounting adjusts for these environmental costs — so that growth achieved by depleting resources and polluting is not counted as pure gain, giving a truer picture of genuine, sustainable progress. This concept supports the pursuit of sustainable development. Understanding green GDP/environmental accounting is a prelims-relevant point. 'Green GDP'/environmental accounting measures growth after accounting for the depletion of natural resources and the cost of environmental damage.

stem: The global set of 17 goals adopted by the United Nations (2015) covering poverty, health, education, environment, etc., to guide sustainable development to 2030, are the:
solution: The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) are the set of 17 global goals adopted by the United Nations (in 2015, as part of the '2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development'), to be achieved by 2030. They cover a broad range of interconnected areas — including ending poverty and hunger, good health and education, gender equality, clean water and sanitation, affordable clean energy, decent work and economic growth, reduced inequalities, sustainable cities, responsible consumption, climate action, protecting life on land and below water, and peace and justice. The SDGs provide a comprehensive global framework/blueprint for pursuing sustainable development — integrating economic, social, and environmental goals — which countries (including India) have committed to work toward. Understanding the SDGs (17 UN goals for sustainable development) is a prelims-relevant point. The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) are 17 UN goals (2015) covering poverty, health, education, environment, etc., to guide sustainable development to 2030.

stem: The 'precautionary principle' in environmental policy holds that:
options: we should wait until harm is fully proven before acting
where an activity may cause serious/irreversible environmental harm, precautionary (preventive) measures should be taken even without full scientific certainty of the harm
solution: The 'precautionary principle' in environmental policy holds that where an activity or substance may cause serious or irreversible harm to the environment (or human health), precautionary (preventive) measures should be taken to avoid or reduce that harm even if the harm has not been fully scientifically proven/established (i.e., even in the face of scientific uncertainty). In other words, 'better safe than sorry' — one should not wait for conclusive proof of harm (by which time the damage may be done and irreversible) before acting to prevent it. This principle is important for dealing with potential environmental threats (like new chemicals, technologies, or activities) whose full effects are uncertain. Understanding the precautionary principle is a prelims-relevant point. The precautionary principle holds that where serious/irreversible environmental harm is possible, preventive measures should be taken even without full scientific certainty.

stem: The rising demand for resources (from a growing population and consumption) combined with the __________ supply of environmental resources is at the root of the environmental crisis.
solution: The root of the environmental crisis lies in the mismatch between: on one hand, the rising demand for environmental resources — driven by the growing population and the increasing consumption (and industrial production) per person; and, on the other hand, the limited/finite supply of environmental resources and the limited capacity of the environment to provide resources and absorb waste (its finite carrying capacity). As the ever-growing demands press against the finite supply and carrying capacity of the environment, the resources get over-exploited and depleted, and pollution/waste accumulates — producing the environmental crisis. So it is the collision of rising demand with a limited environment that causes the problem. Understanding this (rising demand vs finite/limited supply) is a prelims point. The environmental crisis arises from rising demand (growing population and consumption) pressing against the limited/finite supply of environmental resources.

stem: A special environmental challenge for a developing country like India is that it must pursue development to reduce poverty, while also:
options: protecting the environment (facing the twin pressures of development needs and environmental limits)
solution: A special environmental challenge for a developing country like India is that it faces the twin (dual) pressures of development and the environment: on one hand, India must pursue rapid economic development and growth — to reduce its widespread poverty and raise the living standards of its huge population (development is a pressing need); but, on the other hand, it must do so while protecting the environment (facing environmental limits and problems) — because reckless development would degrade the environment (harming the poor, who depend directly on natural resources, and the future). So India must find a way to develop AND protect the environment at the same time — which is exactly the challenge of sustainable development (development that lifts people out of poverty without destroying the environment). Balancing these can be difficult (e.g., poverty itself can drive people to over-use resources, and development pressures can lead to pollution). Understanding this development-vs-environment challenge for India is a prelims-relevant point. India must pursue development to reduce poverty while also protecting the environment — the twin challenge of sustainable development.

stem: The over-extraction and pollution of the environment impose costs on society such as health problems (illness from pollution) and the loss of resources; these are the __________ of environmental degradation.
solution: The over-extraction and pollution of the environment impose real costs (often hidden/uncounted) on society — these are the costs of environmental degradation. They include: health costs — the illnesses and deaths caused by pollution (respiratory and other diseases from air pollution, water-borne diseases from water pollution), and the resulting medical expenses and loss of productivity; the loss of resources and livelihoods (as forests, fisheries, soil, and water are degraded/depleted); the cost of cleaning up and restoring the damaged environment; and the harm from disasters (like floods worsened by deforestation) and from climate change. These costs (borne by society, and especially by the poor) are often not reflected in market prices or conventional GDP (they are 'externalities'/hidden costs) — but they are real and large. Recognising and accounting for these costs is important for making the case for environmental protection and sustainable development. Understanding the costs of environmental degradation is a prelims point. Environmental degradation imposes hidden costs on society — health problems from pollution, the loss of resources, and clean-up costs.

stem: The Chipko movement (hugging trees to prevent deforestation) is a famous example of __________ for environmental protection.
solution: The Chipko movement (in which villagers, especially women, in the Himalayan region hugged the trees to physically prevent them from being cut down by contractors) is a famous example of grassroots/people's action (public participation) for environmental protection. It shows that ordinary people and communities — not just the government — can play a powerful role in protecting the environment (in this case, saving the forests on which their lives depended), through non-violent collective action. It highlights the importance of public awareness, community participation, and people's movements in environmental conservation and sustainable development. Understanding the Chipko movement (as grassroots environmental action) is a prelims-relevant point. The Chipko movement (tree-hugging to prevent deforestation) is a famous example of grassroots people's action for environmental protection.

stem: The disposal of discarded electronic devices (old computers, phones, TVs), which contain toxic materials, poses the growing environmental problem of:
solution: E-waste (electronic waste) is the growing environmental problem posed by the disposal of discarded electronic devices and gadgets — old computers, mobile phones, televisions, printers, batteries, and other electronic/electrical equipment. E-waste is a serious problem because these devices contain toxic and hazardous materials (like lead, mercury, cadmium, and other harmful substances) that, if not properly handled and disposed of, leak into and pollute the soil, water, and air, harming health and the environment. With the rapid growth of electronics use, the amount of e-waste is rising fast, making its safe management (through proper recycling and disposal) an important environmental challenge. Understanding e-waste (as a growing environmental problem) is a prelims-relevant point. E-waste is the growing environmental problem of disposing of discarded electronic devices, which contain toxic materials.

stem: A major source of land and marine pollution, made of non-biodegradable material that persists in the environment for a very long time, is:
solution: Plastic waste is a major source of land and marine (ocean) pollution. Plastic is a non-biodegradable material — it does not decompose/break down naturally (or takes hundreds of years to do so), so it persists in the environment for a very long time, accumulating as litter on land and in water bodies. Plastic waste chokes drains and rivers, litters the land and the seas (huge amounts of plastic end up in the oceans, harming marine life — animals eat or get entangled in it, and it breaks into 'microplastics'), and is difficult to dispose of (burning it releases toxic fumes). Reducing plastic use (and banning single-use plastics), reusing, and recycling are needed to tackle this problem. Understanding plastic waste as a persistent pollutant is a prelims-relevant point. Plastic waste is a major, non-biodegradable pollutant of land and sea that persists in the environment for a very long time.

stem: Which of the following is a strategy for the sustainable use of forests (allowing use while conserving them)?
options: afforestation (planting trees), controlled/selective harvesting, and community/joint forest management
solution: Strategies for the sustainable use of forests — using them to meet needs while conserving them for the future — include: afforestation and reforestation (planting trees to make up for those cut, and to increase the forest cover); controlled and selective harvesting (cutting trees only at a sustainable rate — no faster than they can regrow — and selectively, rather than clear-felling whole forests); protecting forests from fires, encroachment, and over-grazing; and involving local communities in managing and protecting the forests (through Joint Forest Management, which shares responsibility and benefits with the villagers who depend on the forests). These strategies allow forests to be used sustainably (yielding timber, fuel, and other products) while ensuring they are conserved and renewed — an important part of sustainable development. Understanding sustainable forest-use strategies is a prelims-relevant point. Sustainable forest use includes afforestation, controlled/selective harvesting, and community/joint forest management.

stem: The over-use of the environment's function of 'absorbing waste' beyond its capacity results in:
options: the accumulation of pollution/waste (as the environment can no longer absorb and neutralise it all)
solution: The environment has a function of absorbing/assimilating waste — breaking down and neutralising a certain amount of the waste and pollution generated by human activity (acting as a 'sink'). But this absorptive capacity is limited. When we generate waste and pollution faster than the environment can absorb and neutralise it (over-using this function beyond its capacity), the result is the accumulation of pollution and waste — it builds up in the air, water, and land (since the environment can no longer clean it all up), degrading the environment and causing the pollution problems we see (dirty air and water, mounting garbage, etc.). So exceeding the environment's absorptive/carrying capacity for waste leads to pollution build-up. Understanding this is a prelims point. Over-using the environment's waste-absorbing capacity results in the accumulation of pollution/waste, as the environment can no longer absorb it all.

stem: Achieving sustainable development requires the combined efforts of:
options: governments, industries/businesses, and individuals/communities all together (through policies, cleaner technologies, and responsible behaviour)
solution: Achieving sustainable development requires the combined efforts of everyone — governments, industries/businesses, and individuals/communities — all working together. Governments must frame and enforce environmental policies, laws, and standards, invest in clean infrastructure (like renewable energy), and run conservation programmes; industries and businesses must adopt cleaner, more efficient technologies, control their pollution and waste, and use resources responsibly; and individuals and communities must adopt responsible, sustainable behaviour (conserving energy and water, reducing/reusing/recycling, avoiding wasteful consumption, and participating in conservation). Since the environmental crisis is caused by the actions of all of society, tackling it and achieving sustainability also requires action at all these levels together (plus international cooperation for global problems). Understanding that sustainable development needs everyone's combined effort is a prelims-relevant point. Sustainable development requires the combined efforts of governments, industries, and individuals/communities — through policies, cleaner technologies, and responsible behaviour.

stem: Assertion (A): India needs to shift toward renewable energy and cleaner technologies. Reason (R): This would reduce pollution and the depletion of fossil fuels, supporting sustainable development, while still meeting the country's energy needs. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that India needs to shift toward renewable energy (solar, wind, hydro, bio-gas) and cleaner technologies. And the reason is (R) that doing so would reduce pollution (renewables and clean technologies pollute far less than fossil fuels) and reduce the depletion of the finite fossil fuels (coal, oil, gas) — thus supporting sustainable development (protecting the environment and conserving resources for the future) — while still meeting the country's growing energy needs (renewables can supply energy for development). So, because it delivers energy for development while cutting pollution and conserving resources, the shift to renewables/clean technology supports sustainable development — R correctly explains why India needs to make this shift (A). Understanding this reasoning is a prelims point. India should shift to renewable energy and cleaner technologies because this reduces pollution and fossil-fuel depletion (supporting sustainable development) while still meeting energy needs.

stem: In economics, the environment is defined as the totality of all the __________ surroundings of living beings.
solution: The environment is the sum total of all the biotic (plants, animals, microbes) and abiotic (air, water, land, sunlight) surroundings that support and influence life.

stem: The maximum rate at which resources can be used and waste absorbed by the environment without harming it is called its:
solution: The carrying capacity of the environment is its capacity to supply resources and absorb waste without being degraded; problems arise when demands exceed it.

stem: When the rate of resource extraction exceeds the rate of regeneration, and waste generation exceeds the environment's absorptive capacity, the environment fails to perform its function of:
solution: When demands exceed carrying capacity, the environment can no longer perform its vital functions of supplying resources, absorbing waste and sustaining life, leading to an environmental crisis.

stem: Which of the following is a RENEWABLE resource?
solution: Renewable resources (forests, fisheries, water, solar energy) can be replenished by natural processes if used within limits; coal, petroleum and minerals are non-renewable.

stem: Which of the following is a NON-renewable resource?
solution: Petroleum is non-renewable — it takes millions of years to form and gets exhausted with use, unlike renewable solar, wind and forest resources.

stem: The famous definition of sustainable development, 'development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs', comes from the __________ Commission report 'Our Common Future' (1987).
solution: The Brundtland Commission (World Commission on Environment and Development), in its 1987 report 'Our Common Future', gave the classic definition of sustainable development.

stem: The idea that sustainable development requires fairness BETWEEN generations (not depleting resources at the expense of future generations) is called __________ equity.
solution: Inter-generational equity — fairness between present and future generations — is central to sustainable development, requiring that resources be conserved for those to come.

stem: Pollution is a 'negative externality' because the polluter imposes a cost on __________ that the polluter does not pay for.
solution: Pollution is a negative externality: the polluter imposes health and environmental costs on society (third parties) without bearing those costs himself.

stem: The principle that those who cause pollution should bear the cost of the damage/cleanup is called the __________ principle.
solution: The 'polluter pays' principle holds that the party responsible for pollution should bear the cost of managing it and compensating for the damage.

stem: The problem in which a resource open to all (a 'commons', like common grazing land or a fishery) is over-used and degraded because no one owns or protects it is called the:
solution: The 'tragedy of the commons' describes how a shared, open-access resource is over-exploited and degraded because individuals pursue their own interest without responsibility for the whole.

stem: The Earth Summit (UN Conference on Environment and Development) that gave a major boost to sustainable development was held in 1992 in:
solution: The 1992 Earth Summit was held in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil; it produced Agenda 21 and major agreements on sustainable development and climate.

stem: The global set of 17 goals adopted by the UN in 2015 to guide sustainable development to 2030 are called the:
solution: The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) are 17 goals adopted by the UN in 2015, covering poverty, health, education, environment and more, to be achieved by 2030.

stem: The rise in the Earth's average temperature due to increasing greenhouse gases (like carbon dioxide) is called:
solution: Global warming is the rise in the Earth's average temperature caused by the accumulation of greenhouse gases (CO2, methane, etc.) that trap heat in the atmosphere.

stem: The thinning of the ozone layer, caused mainly by chemicals like CFCs, is a problem because the ozone layer protects us from harmful __________ radiation.
solution: The ozone layer shields the Earth from the Sun's harmful ultraviolet (UV) rays; its depletion by CFCs increases skin cancer, cataracts and ecological damage.

stem: The environmental problem in which rainwater becomes acidic (due to gases like sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides), damaging plants, water bodies and buildings, is called:
solution: Acid rain forms when sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides (from burning fossil fuels) dissolve in rainwater, harming forests, lakes, soils and buildings.

stem: The gradual turning of fertile land into desert due to overuse, drought and deforestation is called:
solution: Desertification is the degradation of once-fertile land into barren desert-like conditions, a serious form of land degradation in parts of India.

stem: The Green Revolution, while boosting food output, harmed the environment through:
options: excessive use of chemical fertilisers/pesticides, over-extraction of groundwater, and soil degradation
solution: The Green Revolution's intensive use of chemical fertilisers, pesticides and groundwater led to soil degradation, water depletion, and pollution — negative environmental effects.

stem: The over-extraction of groundwater (for irrigation and other uses) has caused a serious fall in India's __________.
solution: Excessive pumping of groundwater has caused water tables to fall sharply in many parts of India, threatening water security.

stem: A strategy for sustainable development is to shift to non-conventional (renewable) energy sources, such as:
solution: Using renewable energy — solar, wind, biomass, hydro — reduces reliance on polluting, exhaustible fossil fuels and supports sustainable development.

stem: The '3 Rs' strategy of Reduce, Reuse and Recycle helps sustainable development by:
options: reducing the consumption of resources and the generation of waste
solution: The 3 Rs (Reduce, Reuse, Recycle) conserve resources and cut down waste, lowering the pressure on the environment.

stem: The use of bio-gas plants (producing gas from cow-dung and organic waste) in rural areas is a sustainable strategy because it:
options: provides clean fuel and manure from waste, reducing the use of firewood and chemical fertilisers
solution: Bio-gas plants convert cattle dung and organic waste into clean cooking fuel and organic manure, reducing deforestation (firewood use) and dependence on chemical fertilisers.

stem: The traditional Indian practice of harvesting and storing rainwater for later use, which supports sustainable water management, is called:
solution: Rainwater harvesting — collecting and storing rainwater — is a traditional, sustainable method of water conservation and groundwater recharge.

stem: Efficient irrigation methods that save water compared with flooding the fields include drip irrigation and __________ irrigation.
solution: Drip and sprinkler irrigation deliver water directly and efficiently to plants, using far less water than traditional flood/canal irrigation — important for sustainability.

stem: The requirement that large development projects be assessed in advance for their likely environmental effects is called an:
solution: An Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) evaluates the likely environmental consequences of a proposed project before it is approved, helping to prevent or reduce damage.

stem: The concept of 'green GDP' (environmental accounting) tries to measure economic growth after taking into account:
options: the depletion of natural resources and environmental degradation
solution: Green GDP / environmental accounting adjusts conventional GDP for the loss of natural resources and the costs of environmental degradation, giving a truer picture of sustainable growth.

stem: The international solar alliance co-founded by India to promote solar energy worldwide is the:
solution: The International Solar Alliance (ISA), co-founded by India, promotes the use of solar energy among sunshine-rich countries to combat climate change.

stem: India's framework to address climate change through eight national missions (on solar energy, energy efficiency, water, etc.) is the National Action Plan on:
solution: The National Action Plan on Climate Change (NAPCC) comprises eight national missions (including the National Solar Mission and missions on energy efficiency and water) to tackle climate change.

stem: The government's mission to clean and rejuvenate the river Ganga is called:
solution: Namami Gange is the flagship programme to clean and rejuvenate the river Ganga through pollution control, sewage treatment and conservation.

stem: The nationwide campaign for cleanliness and sanitation (building toilets, ending open defecation, managing waste) is the __________ Mission.
solution: The Swachh Bharat Mission is the national cleanliness and sanitation campaign aimed at ending open defecation and improving solid-waste management.

stem: Air pollution in Indian cities (e.g. Delhi) is caused largely by:
options: vehicle emissions, industrial smoke, construction dust and crop-residue burning
solution: Urban air pollution comes mainly from vehicle exhaust, industrial emissions, construction dust and, seasonally, the burning of crop residue (stubble).

stem: The disposal of discarded electronic devices (old computers, phones, TVs), which contain toxic materials, is the growing problem of:
solution: E-waste (electronic waste) is the fast-growing stream of discarded electronic products, which contain hazardous substances requiring safe disposal and recycling.

stem: A major source of land and marine pollution, made of non-biodegradable material that persists for a very long time, is:
solution: Plastic waste, being non-biodegradable, persists in the environment for hundreds of years, polluting land and oceans and harming wildlife.

stem: The loss of the variety of plant and animal species (due to habitat destruction, pollution etc.) is called the loss of:
solution: Loss of biodiversity is the decline in the variety of living species and ecosystems, undermining the environment's stability and services.

stem: The Chipko movement (villagers hugging trees to stop felling) is a famous example of:
options: people's participation/grassroots action for environmental protection
solution: The Chipko movement is a celebrated example of community/grassroots action for environmental conservation, resisting deforestation in the Himalayas.

stem: A special environmental challenge for a developing country like India is that it must:
options: pursue development to reduce poverty while ALSO protecting the environment (balancing the two)
solution: India faces the dual challenge of pursuing economic development to reduce poverty while simultaneously protecting the environment — the essence of sustainable development.

stem: The over-use of the environment's function of ABSORBING waste, beyond its capacity, results in:
options: pollution (accumulation of waste that the environment cannot absorb)
solution: When waste generation exceeds the environment's absorptive capacity, the excess waste accumulates as pollution, damaging air, water and land.

stem: The costs that environmental degradation imposes on society (like illness from pollution and loss of resources) are examples of the __________ of degradation.
solution: Environmental degradation imposes social (external) costs — health problems, loss of resources, cleanup expenses — that are borne by society rather than by the polluter alone.

stem: The root cause of the environmental crisis is the growing __________ for resources combined with the limited (finite) supply and absorptive capacity of the environment.
solution: Rising demand for resources — driven by population growth and higher consumption — pressing against the environment's finite supply and absorptive capacity is the fundamental cause of the crisis.

stem: Sustainable development requires balancing economic development with:
solution: Sustainable development means pursuing economic growth in a way that protects the environment and conserves resources for present and future generations.

stem: Deforestation is an environmental problem because forests __________.
options: provide oxygen, absorb carbon dioxide, conserve soil and water, and shelter biodiversity
solution: Forests supply oxygen, absorb CO2, prevent soil erosion, regulate the water cycle and harbour biodiversity, so their destruction (deforestation) causes serious environmental harm.

stem: Which of the following is a NEGATIVE externality associated with a factory?
options: Emitting smoke and effluents that harm the health of nearby residents
solution: A factory that emits smoke and discharges effluents imposes health and environmental costs on nearby residents — a negative externality (pollution).

stem: The 'carrying capacity' of the environment implies that resources should be used at a rate that:
options: does not exceed the rate of their natural regeneration/replenishment
solution: Respecting carrying capacity means using renewable resources no faster than they regenerate and generating waste no faster than the environment can absorb it.

stem: An example of a sustainable, decentralised energy solution suitable for remote villages is:
options: rooftop solar panels / mini solar grids
solution: Solar power (rooftop panels, mini-grids) offers a clean, decentralised, renewable energy solution well suited to remote and rural areas, supporting sustainable development.

stem: Which of the following BEST captures the central message of the chapter on environment and sustainable development?
options: Development and the environment are interlinked, so growth must be sustainable — meeting present needs without harming the ability of future generations to meet theirs
solution: The chapter concludes that economic development and the environment are deeply interlinked, and that development must be sustainable — meeting present needs without degrading the environment or compromising future generations.

stem: The overall message of the chapter 'Environment and Sustainable Development' is that:
options: The environment does not matter for the economy

The environment provides the resources and life-support on which the economy and life depend, but human demands (from rising population and consumption) have exceeded its carrying capacity, causing an environmental crisis (pollution, resource depletion, global warming) — so development must become 'sustainable', meeting present needs without harming the environment or the ability of future generations to meet theirs
We should use up all resources now
solution: The chapter conveys that the environment — the total planetary inheritance of biotic and abiotic elements — provides the essential resources (both renewable and non-renewable) and the life-support functions (supplying resources, absorbing waste, sustaining life, and providing aesthetic and other services) on which the economy and all life depend. It explains that the environment can perform these functions without harm only so long as the demands placed on it stay within its 'carrying capacity'; but that the enormous rise in population, consumption, and industrial activity has caused the demands on the environment to exceed its carrying capacity, leading to a serious environmental crisis — including the over-exploitation and depletion of resources (deforestation, groundwater depletion, exhaustion of minerals/fossil fuels), the degradation of land (erosion, desertification), and severe pollution of air, water, and land, as well as the great global problems of global warming/climate change and ozone depletion. The chapter emphasises that, because the current path of resource-degrading, polluting development is unsustainable (it undermines its own future basis and harms present and future generations), development must be made 'sustainable' — defined as development that meets the needs of the present generation without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs, by balancing economic development with environmental protection and social equity. It outlines strategies for sustainable development — such as using non-conventional/renewable energy (solar, wind, hydro, bio-gas), conserving resources (the 3 Rs — Reduce, Reuse, Recycle, and rainwater harvesting), promoting sustainable and organic agriculture, controlling pollution, and using cleaner technologies. Understanding the environment's functions and carrying capacity, the causes and forms of the environmental crisis, and the meaning, importance, and strategies of sustainable development is the central concern of this chapter. The environment sustains the economy and life, but human demands have exceeded its carrying capacity, causing an environmental crisis — so development must become sustainable, meeting present needs without harming the environment or future generations.
